item.title: How the Brain Knows When It’s Time for Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

How the Brain Knows When It’s Time for Sleep

You can postpone sleep, but only for so long.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Brain cells in mice become increasingly active during prolonged wakefulness and help encourage sleep.
  • Turning these cells on caused mice to sleep longer and more deeply.
  • Suppressing these cells dramatically reduced sleepiness, even after hours awake.
  • When two populations of these cells were chronically suppressed, mice slept nearly 70% less.

You can postpone sleep, but only for so long. After a late night, the eyelids grow heavy, attention slips, and eventually staying awake begins to feel impossible. The longer we resist, the stronger the need for sleep becomes.

Where does this accumulating pressure come from? Does the brain simply become exhausted? Does some chemical gradually accumulate? Or is there a system inside the brain that actively keeps track of how long we have been awake?

A new study published in Nature offers striking evidence for the last possibility. By examining the brains of sleep-deprived mice, the study identifies particular groups of neurons that become increasingly active during wakefulness. These cells may be counting down the hours until bedtime.

Finding the Brain's Sleep Meter

Mice normally sleep during much of the day and become more active at night. To see what changes as sleep pressure rises, the mice were kept awake for six hours during the period when they would ordinarily rest.

Some mice were kept occupied by grooming-related stimulation, while others were given unfamiliar objects to explore. Afterward, the study mapped activity throughout the brain. Three broad patterns appeared. Some areas responded strongly at the beginning of sleep deprivation, probably because the animals were encountering new stimulation. Other areas became active during recovery sleep. But a third set behaved differently: Activity rose or remained elevated as the mice stayed awake, then declined once they were finally allowed to sleep.

One brain region activated in this process, called the median raphe, lies deep in the brainstem. Another sits farther forward in a part of the brain involved in sleep regulation and body maintenance, called the anterior medial preoptic area.

Their activity did not increase only during forced sleep deprivation. It also followed the animals' ordinary daily pattern. The cells became more active during periods when mice naturally spent more time awake and less active during periods dominated by sleep. That made them compelling candidates for something more fundamental than a response to an experiment. Their activity seemed to follow sleep need itself.

Turning Up the Sleep Pressure

These sleep-deprivation-responsive cells were marked and later reactivated when the mice were well rested. Activating these cells in either of the two brain regions caused the mice to spend roughly two to three times more time asleep. Their sleep also became deeper, based on the large, slow brain waves associated with intense non-rapid eye movement sleep. The animals were behaving as though they had accumulated a substantial sleep debt, even though they had not.

Suppressing the same cells produced essentially the opposite result. Mice slept less during ordinary conditions and could remain awake for unusually long stretches. During another six-hour period of sleep deprivation, they made fewer attempts to fall asleep. In some cases, suppressing cells in the median raphe eliminated these attempts almost entirely. Even when the animals were finally given the opportunity to recover, they slept less than normal.

Many things can keep an animal awake. Stimulants, stress, or activation of the brain's arousal systems can all delay sleep. But the lost sleep usually has to be paid back later. Sleep pressure continues building beneath the temporary wakefulness. However, suppressing these particular neurons appeared to reduce the pressure itself.

Two populations emerged as especially important for promoting sleep. One uses serotonin, a chemical messenger involved in a wide range of brain functions. The other is an inhibitory population, meaning that its normal role involves restraining the activity of other neurons. Activating either population increased deep sleep. Activating both at the same time produced a much stronger effect that lasted longer than stimulating either one alone. As wakefulness continues, these neurons themselves may become easier to activate. Eventually, the system increasingly favors sleep.

When the Sleep Dial Was Turned Down

When the sleep-controlling neurons were suppressed for weeks rather than hours, the surviving mice slept nearly 70% less than control animals. They spent more than six additional hours awake each day and could remain awake for much longer stretches at a time.

Ordinarily, losing that much sleep should create enormous sleep pressure. Yet the expected signs were greatly reduced. The mice showed less of the deep, slow brain activity normally associated with accumulated sleep need. After deliberate sleep deprivation, they did not show the usual surge of recovery sleep.

They also remained remarkably active. Their movement actually increased, and they continued exploring and interacting with objects. Memory was somewhat weaker one day after learning, but the animals still formed lasting memories, and by two weeks their performance was comparable with that of control mice.

About 17% of the mice subjected to the long-term intervention died, possibly because sleep had been reduced even further in those animals. The surviving mice were also genetically and neurologically manipulated in a highly specific way.

Why We Get Sleepy May Be as Important as Why We Sleep

Sleep is often described as something the brain needs to perform maintenance, consolidate memories, regulate metabolism, or restore normal function. Those ideas address an important question: Why sleep at all?

This study approaches a different question: Why does the need for sleep become so difficult to resist? The answer may involve a set of neurons that spend our waking hours moving the brain progressively closer to sleep. Cells in the median raphe appear capable of influencing other parts of the brain that control whether we remain awake or fall asleep. Some of their connections activate sleep-promoting regions while suppressing areas involved in wakefulness.

The urge to sleep may not simply be a symptom of a tired brain. It may be a biological drive built by specialized neural circuits, much like the systems that make hunger grow when we have not eaten or thirst intensify when we need water.

Every hour we remain awake, something inside the brain may be keeping score. And when that score tips over a certain threshold, sleep is no longer a matter of choice.

item.title: The Many Meanings of Making Love
item.description:
Relationships

The Many Meanings of Making Love

Personal Perspective: An expansive view of making love enhances shared pleasure.

Posted October 29, 2026

Source: PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Most of us have grown up with the notion that “making love” means having sex. And, at its best, that’s what sex can be. But making love can also mean much more.

My late friend Elizabeth Kanitz Canfield, a health educator and activist and an Austrian Holocaust survivor, was adamant in her belief that most people see making love in an all-too-limited way, relegating the concept solely to the physical, sexual realm when it could be expanded to mean so many ways people can share pleasure and, in so doing, increase the intensity of their emotional bond with each other.

“Listening to music together and being transported by the beauty of it is making love,” Liz would insist. “Taking a hike together and reveling in all the sights, sounds, and smells of the outdoors with pleasure and gratitude is making love. A good conversation, where you really connect with another, is making love.”

This expanded concept of making love can be a blessing in a number of circumstances:

It can further bond a romantic couple with a greater variety of shared pleasures.

It can deepen ties with close friends who will never be lovers but who can share love and delight in mutual interests and experiences.

It can become a soothing, reassuring substitute for physical lovemaking as a couple ages. For some, cuddling while listening to favorite music or revisiting favorite places or simply sharing warm memories is love-enhancing.

In our closest relationships, both sexual and platonic, allowing ourselves to have experiences that please all of our senses can help to create a lasting bond of shared pleasure.

What are your varied ways of making love?

Perhaps making love is enjoying a brisk walk in the chill of late autumn or reverting to your shared childhood passion of making snow angels and laughing as you enjoy the first snow of winter.

Perhaps making love is swimming with someone special in a tropical lagoon—or a backyard pool.

Perhaps making love is delighting in the antics and laughter of a child you share.

Or it may be embracing and reconnecting after a period of emotional distance, sharing both relief and joy that your relationship is enduring.

Making love may mean shared laughter, finding humor in everyday events, in resolved crises, or in memories.

I close my eyes and remember my dear friend Maurice, whose lighthearted humor and contagious laughter made him a delightful companion, both as a lover and, later on, as a lifelong platonic friend. Like Liz, Maurice was a Holocaust survivor (of the infamous Baghdad Farhud). He managed the trauma of that time by laughing between the tears and moments of pain and lived a long life filled not only with painful memories, but also true joy. Laughing with him was making love.

Both Liz and Maurice, who witnessed and experienced unspeakable horrors in their youth, lived fully and joyously, embracing pleasures both simple and profound that they readily shared with others.

To be able to do the same is truly making love.

item.title: What Conversations in Dreams Say About Our Sleeping Minds
item.description:
Dreaming

What Conversations in Dreams Say About Our Sleeping Minds

Dream characters are products of our brains, but we can't predict what they'll say.

Posted October 29, 2026

Imagine walking up to someone and asking them a simple math question. Instead of answering, they burst into tears, run away, or tell you the answer is too personal to share.

Now imagine that person doesn’t exist. They’re a character in your dream, a product of your own brain.

Almost every night, we interact with people who exist only in our minds. They talk, argue, laugh, and sometimes behave in ways that catch us entirely by surprise. But here's a fascinating question: If our brains are creating these characters, why don't we know what they're going to say? How can our own brain surprise us every single night?

A handful of wonderfully creative studies have explored this question by asking lucid dreamers—people who know they are dreaming while still asleep—to strike up conversations with their imaginary companions and report what happened.

In an early study, one dreamer asked a character whether it had consciousness. The response? “I am sure that I have a consciousness, but I doubt if you have one, because you ask me such stupid questions!” Cheeky!

Dream Characters Are Terrible at Math (and Sometimes Very Sensitive About It)

In a 2010 pilot study, researchers asked lucid dreamers to seek out a wise “guide” in their dream to help them tackle puzzles or invent metaphors1.

The dream guides were not exactly logic champions: They supplied just one correct answer in 11 encounters involving logical puzzles. However, their advice on creative tasks was more promising. When asked to produce metaphors for unlikely scenes like a child playing in a cemetery, a dream guide responded, “a flower growing on waste land.” Not bad for a made-up character. The authors summarized their pilot study with an intriguing conclusion: Dream characters may be more helpful with imaginative associations than with step-by-step logic.

To follow up on this idea, the researchers conducted another study in which they instructed lucid dreamers to ask their characters if they could solve simple arithmetic problems2.

Here again, dream characters were not particularly gifted mathematicians. They got only about a third of their responses correct, even struggling with calculations as simple as 3+4.

But their reactions to the questions were even more interesting. When asked to solve 8+2, one dream character appeared irritated, as though the dreamer had asked something forbidden, before delivering the mysterious response, "Gray zone."

Another character, asked to calculate 18 minus 6, refused to answer, apparently treating the result as highly confidential information. In other dreams, characters simply fled the scene. One even started crying.

Apparently, being asked to do mental arithmetic can be just as unpleasant for imaginary people as it is for real ones.

From brain imaging data, we know that solving mathematical calculations involves a set of regions in the frontal and parietal parts of the brain. During REM sleep, in which lucid dreams typically occur, these regions are relatively deactivated. This might explain why mathematical operations are beyond the reach of the dream world.

Can Dream Characters Read Our Minds?

In 2014, researchers asked lucid dreamers to perform a different task3. They were instructed to hold up a number of fingers behind their backs and ask dream characters to guess how many they were showing.

In waking life, if you were to try to guess how many fingers your friend is holding behind their back (i.e., guessing a number between 0 and 10), you would have roughly a 9 percent chance of getting it right.

In the dream world, however, characters correctly identified the hidden number 66 percent of the time. Remarkably, the characters were almost as successful at identifying hidden fingers as they were at counting fingers held directly in front of them.

In a second experiment, the researchers reversed the challenge. Dream characters were asked to write down a number, and dreamers attempted to guess it. The dreamers succeeded in approximately 71 percent of completed trials.

Does this mean dream characters possess extraordinary mind-reading abilities?

Not quite.

After all, both the dreamer and the character are creations of the same sleeping brain. Information that appears hidden from one character may still be accessible to the neural processes generating the entire experience.

These were small, exploratory studies based on self-reported dreams, but they still raise a fascinating question: How does the brain distribute information between the different characters it creates, and why can we access some information about other characters (like in the number guessing task) but stay completely in the dark about their knowledge otherwise?

When Your Imaginary Friends Have Had Enough of You

In the last task I want to share with you, dream researcher Antonio Zadra teamed up with an experienced lucid dreamer and visual artist, Dave Green4. Green spent two years approaching characters in his dreams and asking them to draw something.

You might expect these imaginary artists to be cooperative. After all, they're being generated by the very artistic brain making the request.

You would be wrong.

Several characters were annoyed by the request; two girls giggled and insisted that Green had already asked them to draw on a previous occasion. Another character began writing mathematical equations instead of drawing. When Green pressed her to produce an actual picture, a second character intervened to defend her: "Look mate, you asked the lady to do a drawing and she did one, now leave her alone."

Apparently, even our imaginary friends have boundaries.

Green also experienced more cooperative characters. In one dream, he met a character that looked like a professor. The character said he was in too much of a rush to draw. But then Green explained what the experiment was about, and the character replied, “How fascinating!” and enthusiastically took the pen and started to draw (you can see drawing examples in the fourth reference below). Green even got a golden retriever to produce artwork using its paw.

Interestingly, one character drew an image that appeared upside down from Green's perspective, as though the character was genuinely seeing the page from a first-person point of view. Green’s brain wasn't merely inventing dialogue. It appeared capable of constructing multiple perspectives within the same imaginary world.

Who Is Writing the Script?

These studies reveal something remarkable about dreaming: While we sleep, our brains create elaborate social worlds populated by characters who seem to behave autonomously and independently of the dreamer, guided by their own personalities, emotions, and private thoughts.

And even when we know perfectly well that we're dreaming, we often have no idea what these characters will say next. Think about it: A lucid dreamer has mustered enough consciousness to become aware of the dream and exert volitional control over their own thoughts and behaviors, and still dream characters continue in an almost parallel world inaccessible to even the lucid ones.

This doesn't mean dream characters possess independent consciousness. But it does suggest that the brain can generate complex social interactions outside the dreamer’s conscious awareness.

It is still an open question whether having the brain keep much of the dream “script” outside of our awareness is part of the functional significance of dreams. Some theories suggest that believing our dream experiences and reacting to them in potentially adaptive ways plays a central role in the evolutionary function of dreams. Just as we can never be sure what awaits us next in waking life, dreams are constructed with an unknown future, often even more shifty and unpredictable than wakeful reality.

What these small, exploratory studies demonstrate most clearly is how little we still understand about the extraordinarily rich world our brains create every night.

The next time you find yourself lucid dreaming, try asking someone a question.

Just maybe don't start with math.

item.title: When You Start Keeping Score With Your Cofounder
item.description:
Coaching

When You Start Keeping Score With Your Cofounder

Lost trust between business partners often begins with a story told in private.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Trust between cofounders often erodes through private interpretation, before any open conflict.
  • Our explanations of a partner draw on early relationships as much as on the partner.
  • Each partner's defensive reaction can become evidence for the other's story.
  • How intensely a story feels says little about whether it is accurate or complete.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

You've stopped telling your cofounder when something bothers you. Instead, you're just keeping score: the fundraise that didn't close, the meeting where they talked over you in front of the entire team. And you've already decided why they do it.

That's exactly how trust between cofounders usually dies: One person builds a case, and the other never hears it until it's too late.

When trust erodes between cofounders, the cause is usually not the conflict itself. It's the meaning we assign to it.

When there's full trust and respect, disagreement can feel productive—even generative. Each person leaves the conversation having learned something they didn't have in their heads going into it. But when conflict feels threatening or destabilizing, it erodes trust.

Where the Meaning Comes From

We are meaning-making machines. When our cofounder says or does something that hurts, the first thing we try to do is understand why they did it. You build your explanation from three key things: how you understand people in general, your internal model of your cofounder, and a lot of guesses and inferences to fill in the data points you don't already know.

Because this semiconscious process happens quickly, it's prone to error and bias. Your picture of them is made up of what they've revealed to you—like how they deliver, how they operate, and their reputation—but it mixes with your own history. It creates a composite of who they've shown themselves to be and the expectations you learned from others while you were growing up, like whether people are reliable or fundamentally unreliable. That composite is more fixed and rigid than the real person in front of you. They keep changing and evolving. Your internal model usually hasn't caught up.

When the Stories Interlock

Once a story takes root, it stops being open to change. You and your cofounder each probably have these stories about one another, and the problem is that they interlock. Each person's defense becomes the other person's evidence.

Let me give you an example. Aisha, the CEO, sees her CTO, Tom, as underperforming. She criticizes his performance and the performance of the engineering team, and Tom emotionally withdraws. He starts speaking less in meetings. He disengages a little. Now her story is confirmed: Tom lacks commitment and needs to be replaced. Tom's story is that Aisha wants him out of the company, and that feels truer than at any point in the past, when all Aisha actually wants is more engagement and performance.

The researchers Kathleen Kennedy and Emily Pronin (2008) call this the bias-perception conflict spiral. When you see someone who disagrees with you as biased, you get more confrontational, and the more confrontational you become, the more biased you look to them.

Between cofounders, the moment you decide their motives are bad, you fight harder. You become more aggressive and accusatory, and then you become the bad actor in their story. Sometimes both people disengage instead, and decisions stall. Once you're in that kind of gridlock, every interaction feels compromised from the start.

Co-Authoring a Fuller Story

The goal as a cofounding team is to co-author a fuller, more holistic story than either of you can in isolation. The narrative therapists Michael White and David Epston (1990) described thin and thick descriptions.

  • A thin description reduces a person to a problem: She never listens. He's selfish.
  • A thick description includes history, context, and what each person cares about.

Between cofounders, a lot of the work is thickening the story together. If Dan sees Maya as overly cautious and Maya sees Dan as impulsive, the story they could build together is that they have different levels of risk tolerance they've never made explicit. Once they do, they can decide when to lean into Maya's caution, when to lean into Dan's speed, and when to use a hybrid.

In practice, I coach cofounders to break the story in four moves. Say my cofounder, Mark, interrupted me three times in an all-hands meeting.

  1. I state the observation—the shared observable reality Mark would agree with: He interrupted me three times. Not that he's someone who doesn't care about my opinion, because that's my judgment and my story.
  2. I name the impact with an I-message: "When you interrupted me those three times, I felt frustrated, because I value us presenting a united front. Would you be open to syncing more beforehand next time?" If you're on the receiving end, own the impact first. You can clarify your intent later.
  3. If the story is taking up too much real estate in my mind, I share it as a story: "Mark, the story I'm telling myself is that you care a lot about what other people think and don't always value my input." That usually reveals the gap between my story and his internal reality.
  4. We update the narrative. Maybe Mark felt anxious that the team lacked context, so he jumped in, and we both want to align before the next all-hands because we both care about presenting a united front.

Every month that you keep score without saying anything, that story gets harder to change. And the company pays for it in the decisions the two of you aren't making together.

item.title: Protect Your Relationship From Social Media Misinformation
item.description:
Social Media

Protect Your Relationship From Social Media Misinformation

How to regain control of what you see in your feed.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Social media algorithms are neutral tools, but they can direct your attention in ways you didn’t anticipate.
  • The way you engage with these algorithms can expose you to relationship content that’s misinformative.
  • Learning to diversify the content you’re shown can help you take back control of your feed.
Source: Maya Lab / Shutterstock

Co-authored by Nick Lane

This is Part 3 of a three-part series.

It’s well established that what we see on social media can shape the way we think about relationships. What we didn’t know when we began this series was whether social media could have something to do with why so many people are choosing to opt out of dating and relationships altogether. In our first post on this topic, we uncovered differences in the content that men and women were exposed to in their feeds. In our second post, we explored the potential for divisiveness created by the types of relationship misinformation we encountered. Now, we want you to know that you aren’t at the mercy of what your algorithm is showing you. In this final post, we’ll share ways you can gain a new perspective on relationships by breaking out of the algorithmic echo chamber that we’ve described.

Understanding Your Algorithm

An algorithm is a tool. We often forget that. It’s not inherently good or bad. An algorithm is specifically designed to provide an individualized user experience. Regardless of whether it's positive or negative, an algorithm is simply doing its job by showing you things that capture your attention. It operates by using some combination of collaborative or content-based filtering, which makes recommendations based on the preferences of users similar to you or based on your own past preferences, respectively. The point is that an algorithm rarely shows you content completely at random.

The downside of an algorithm is that it sometimes restricts what a user sees so much that it creates a filter bubble, which can limit exposure to diverse perspectives. When the same type of content is blasted to you on repeat, there is the potential for it to bias your beliefs and make outlier experiences seem more common than what they actually are.

Retraining Your Algorithm

To figure out why certain relationship content keeps being recommended to you, it can help to reflect on what you do online. In one illustrative data science simulation, when a user who consumed mostly sports news suddenly showed an interest in three political news stories, it was enough to change the political content of their feed by 27 percentage points, from 13 percent to 40 percent politics. If you want to change what you see, you have to engage with more of the content you want and less of what you don’t. Here are a few examples of questions you can ask yourself:

  • Is the content I’m seeing only showing me the negative behaviors of others in relationships?
  • Does this content make me want to put more effort into my relationships, or less?
  • Is this content encouraging me to hold adversarial beliefs about someone I haven’t even met yet, like a potential partner or spouse?
  • Is the same negative message about relationships being repeated to me ad nauseam?
  • Am I having an emotional response to this content or formulating beliefs about relationships based on experiences that are not mine?

When viewing content causes you to relive a bad situation over and over again, it can turn into rumination. And dwelling on an experience doesn’t always create the mental space for perspective, wisdom, or healing. It can also reinforce existing beliefs and may even contribute to polarization through the creation of bias. Here are a few things we learned about how you can break the cycle by retraining your algorithm:

  • Every like, comment, and share signals interest. You endorse content by engaging with it, so hit send only on things you want more of.
  • A follow is a strong signal. Seek out credible sources and follow people who have built a reputation by debunking relationship myths. Remember: Just because it’s trending doesn’t mean it’s true.
  • Hate-watching videos is counterproductive. When you linger on a video or watch to the end, that’s engagement, regardless of whether you liked what you saw. Don’t pause on things you don’t enjoy seeing.
  • Your current behavior is telling. People’s interests can change quickly, and your algorithm knows it. What you’ve been watching lately is going to affect what you see, even if it’s dramatically different from what you’ve been drawn to before.
  • Be purposeful in seeking out healthy relationship ideologies. Search terms like “good communication habits,” “effective conflict management skills,” and “how to date intentionally” can help guide you in the direction of content that aligns with your values.

What It All Means

Many of us have gone through relationship ups and downs. Wanting to learn from those experiences and share them with others is natural but can also lead us to misinformative content. In this series, we’ve described some ways that the content served up by algorithms can inadvertently influence our own beliefs about dating and relationships. We’ve also invited you to consider the kinds of messages about relationships that keep being repeated to you. We hope this series can be the beginning of a dialogue within ourselves and our relationships about how what we’re consuming on social media might be affecting our own desire for real-world connection.

This post was co-authored by Nick Lane, a health care practitioner interested in the intersection between physical and psychological well-being.

item.title: Would Anyone Want Your Job?
item.description:
Leadership

Would Anyone Want Your Job?

Sustainable leaders build their roles so others can actually succeed in them.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • If no one wants to step into your leadership role, the problem may be the job itself, not the successors.
  • A desirable leadership position provides the authority, resources, and support needed to succeed.
  • Reliable systems, fewer emergencies, and empowered colleagues make the job more attractive to the next leader.
  • To lead sustainably, build a leadership role someone else genuinely wants to step into.
An open chair for the next leader.
Source: Jeff Frey / Used with permission

When a nonprofit executive I interviewed told her board she was leaving, they were not happy. Some staff cried. She cared about the organization, too, and understood why the news was hard to hear.

But something else happened. People started asking about the job.

A few years earlier, the position had been a difficult sell. The organization was struggling, and people knew it. An interim leader who had previously decided she didn't want the permanent role was now interested. When the board asked whether she was ready to take over, she said yes. And others were calling to ask about the open position.

“It feels good to know that it’s gotten to a place where people don’t feel like it’s so scary,” the executive told me. This is a great story. In just a few years, a leader had turned the leadership role itself around.

We tend to judge leaders by what they accomplish while they are in the job. What if we also judged them by whether anyone would want that job when they leave?

When the Job Becomes the Problem

Many leadership positions sound great on paper. But in practice, the expectations may be impossible. Every issue rises to the top, the board expects immediate answers, and the leader is responsible for results without enough authority or support.

Eventually, people begin to believe the job requires a special kind of person. Someone who can work all the time, absorb every problem, and somehow remain cheerful about it.

Well…maybe the job is the problem.

Bakker and colleagues (2005) studied over 1,000 employees and found that job resources given to the leader in the role, like autonomy, feedback, and social support, weaken the relationship between demanding work and certain aspects of burnout. The point for leaders is practical: When demands are high, personal determination is not a substitute for a job that gives people what they need to do it.

I interviewed the executive’s spouse as part of my research study. He had watched her work through much of this. He described her ability to look at a struggling organization and “create calm out of chaos.” He also saw the stress, the difficult personnel decisions, and the ways those “pressures sometimes follow her home.”

Pay attention to that. The lesson? An organization can improve while the person improving it pays a steep price. But sustainable leadership has to account for both.

Make the Emergency Ordinary

The executive told me two stories about routine food deliveries that failed to arrive.

The first: Early in her tenure, the missed delivery meant people had to scramble to a grocery store to buy enough bread to keep serving meals. Everyone dropped what they were doing. It was a crisis.

The second: Later, when a delivery problem occurred, the organization had backup food ready. Someone made a phone call, adjusted the plan, and everyone kept moving. Crisis averted.

Same problem. Very different day.

What changed is one of the least glamorous, but most valuable, parts of leadership: finding what repeatedly creates emergencies and making sure they no longer require an emergency response.

Imagine how different that job feels to the next person. There will still be surprises, but fewer problems will require only the executive to solve them.

Give People Room to Lead

People avoid leadership jobs for many reasons, but a big one is that they see every decision having to travel through one exhausted person. The role looks lonely because it is.

A meta-analysis of 105 samples by Lee and colleagues (2018) found that “empowering leadership” was positively associated with employee performance, helping behaviors, and creativity. Basically, giving people meaningful authority in their job can reduce an organization's dependence on one person’s judgment.

In my interview, the important moment was the past interim leader saying she was now willing to fill the role. We cannot know everything that informed her decision, but her answer suggests how the position was perceived. It had become a positive thing rather than a warning.

Succession Is Part of the Job

Most leaders say succession planning matters, but few actually make time for it. Froelich and colleagues (2011) found a gap between nonprofits’ high concern about executive succession and their actual low preparation for it.

And succession cannot rest entirely on the executive’s shoulders. Everyone needs to get involved. In a study of 1,020 nonprofit respondents in Germany, Geib and Boenigk (2022) found that shared accountability for succession planning between the board, the executive, and human resources was associated with a stronger sense of leadership continuity.

That means not just paying attention to the leader, but paying attention to the position itself. Are expectations realistic? Does the leader have authority to match responsibility? Are other people learning to make decisions? Could someone step in without spending the first six months putting out fires?

For the leader, it means taking pride in something hard to see: fewer emergencies, capable colleagues, and work that continues when you are not there.

Would You Take Your Own Job?

Before that executive left, she told me that everyone seemed confident that “nothing was falling through the cracks.” I suspect that reassurance meant a lot to people who worried about what would happen next.

So ask yourself this: If you had to apply for your own job today, knowing what you know about the hours, expectations, support, and pressure, would you take it?

If the answer is no, that's useful information. You probably have some work to do on the job itself, not just on your ability to handle it.

To lead sustainably, build a leadership role someone else wants to step into.

item.title: The Real Reason Your Habits Never Take Root
item.description:
Habit Formation

The Real Reason Your Habits Never Take Root

You're not picking the wrong habit, you just quit before it took root.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • New habits take longer to form than most people give them to take root.
  • Studies show that writing a plan around a new habit explained 40 to 83 percent of its long-term success.
  • Every time you switch a habit, you throw away the progress it made toward becoming automatic.

Devon tried five different morning habits in one year: a tracking app, a five-minute journal, a cold-plunge routine, a meditation app, and a paper planner. No attempt lasted more than two or three weeks before Devon decided it didn’t work. He always came to me with the same conclusion: "I tried the wrong system. I have to find the right one."

Maybe you don't own five apps. But I'd bet you've made this move before: the planner that was supposed to be the one, the workout program swapped before week three.

Every abandoned system teaches you the same lesson twice: that you're someone who starts things and doesn't finish them. And deciding to switch feels like taking action, which is the trap. Why? Because intention moves behavior far less than we assume. An analysis of 47 experiments found that a sizeable jump in what people intend to do produces only about half as large a jump in what they actually do (Webb & Sheeran, 2006).

And that’s despite the fact that the method you pick may matter less than you think it does. In a meta-analysis of 52 randomized trials of cognitive behavioral therapy for addiction, CBT beat usual or minimal care but was no better than any other evidence-based treatment (Magill et al., 2026). That matches what I see in my work: When it comes to good-enough options, staying matters more than choosing.

Making a Plan Makes the Practice Stick

Researchers at UC Berkeley (Susman et al., 2026) recruited 497 adults and taught them the same practice: a private, comforting hand-over-heart gesture, held for 20 seconds. Everyone chose a cue ("when I finish brushing my teeth, I'll do it").

Then they split the groups: Half stopped there, while the other half watched a 15-minute video on habit science and filled out a written plan. They pre-decided when they'd practice, where, what might get in the way, and the payoff the practice would give them. They set a daily phone reminder, got permission for two "skip days" a week, and closed by visualizing the plan.

What did they find? Six months later, the second group practiced more often and more automatically. They also reported more self-compassion and fewer mental health symptoms. Gains in automaticity over the first three months accounted for roughly 40 percent to 83 percent of those six-month differences. The effects were small, but real: about two extra practice sessions a week, roughly a third more practice than the cue-only group.

Importantly, the trial tested the whole package, so it can't say which piece did the work. But I believe that simply setting a vision of who you'll become gives you a future self to measure against, and you come up short of that every single day. But a plan gives you a planned program of repetitions to measure against, and you can hit that today (and tomorrow, until you match that future vision).

You're not weak-willed. You just haven't put in enough reps, in the same place and at the same time, for anything to take root. The "21 days to a habit" figure has no evidence behind it. In one study, new habits took anywhere from 18 to 254 days to become automatic (Lally et al., 2010), roughly three weeks to eight months. Have you given your new habits that much time?

The same thing plays out in many "tried and failed" efforts: the Sunday call to your mother, the workout program restarted every January. Each new start feels difficult before it roots, and you read that difficulty as proof you can't do it, or that you planted the wrong seed. By the fifth time, you start to suspect the problem is you. Devon wasn't really trying a sixth system; he was unsure whether habits even work for him.

Why You Keep Quitting Before It Sticks

So why do smart, motivated people keep switching too early? Here’s what I’ve seen with clients:

Starting feels like doing something. Week one pays off quickly: it's new (releases dopamine), gives a sense of progress, and may even get noticed by others. If enthusiasm got noticed growing up and follow-through didn't, that pull runs even stronger. Nobody claps for week six of the same boring routine.

Comparing options feels responsible. Spending time researching the "right" recovery framework can feel like proof that you care. Many of us were taught, in school or by an achievement-minded parent, that a "right" answer is out there waiting, and researching reads as diligence. But it's procrastination research—aim, aim, aim, but never fire.

The stretch before something roots feels hardest, and that's when you bail. The cost usually shows up well before the payoff. A fruit tree may bear no fruit for two to three years... that's not a sign it won't. If an early setback got treated as proof something was broken when you were younger, that reading is probably still running. You have to learn to sit with the strain and keep going.

Any of those sound familiar?

When Switching Is the Right Call

Does all this mean you should never switch? Not at all. If a practice is making things worse, stop. If a 6 a.m. journal can't survive your night shifts, the fit is the problem. And early on, trying a few options is a reasonable search.

The trick is to switch on purpose. Set a stopping rule before you start: how many weeks you'll give it, and how you'll track success. Then count repetitions, and track whether it's getting easier and moving you toward your goal. If you're just working and nothing is getting better, it may be time to switch. Handled that way, you can make a switch with data, instead of only because it's hard.

How to Write the Plan

A cue tells you when to start, but not where, what might stop you, or why you're bothering. Put all four in one sentence: "At 7 a.m., after coffee, in the kitchen, I will write down three things I'm grateful for in my journal; if the baby's up early, I'll do it on my phone in the baby's room, because noticing the good in my life makes me a better father."

Name the reward and set the reminder before you need either. Decide while you're calm. In my experience, the tired and stressed moments usually win, and you fall back on what's familiar.

Decide what a skip day means before you miss one. An undefined miss can feel like failure, and a broken streak is probably an excuse you've used to start over before. Give yourself two skips a week. Script for the day you miss: "That's one of my two. Tomorrow I'm back on."

Remember This

In simple terms: Give the habit in front of you a full plan, a fair number of weeks, and a way to see whether it's working. The strain in week two is the friction growth requires; your tracking tells you whether this habit is worth it. I've done plenty of switching myself. We're all human, after all.

What's the one habit you'd write the whole plan for this week?

If this pattern sounds familiar, my book Unhooked goes deeper into what makes change durable. A fuller evidence review of why willpower isn't the mechanism lives here.

item.title: Becoming Dada: What Keeps a Father There
item.description:
Parenting

Becoming Dada: What Keeps a Father There

A neuroscientist asks what caring for his son may be changing in his biology.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • Animal studies show that caregiving circuits can be reorganized in fathers.
  • Imaging studies show changes in fathers' brain structure after birth.
  • Testosterone tends to fall when men become partnered fathers; fathers who do more childcare have lower levels.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

My toddler son still comes to me when he is upset and says, “Tell me a story.” In Part 1, I wrote about how reward, touch, and a familiar sentence draw me into this ritual. Here I write about the staying, and about what fatherhood may be doing to a father’s brain over time.

I stay with him

Comforting my son also means managing my own response while trying to understand his. I feel mostly tenderness; I let that set the pace. My voice slows and stays low, even when the crying does not. Sometimes the story is not enough, and the approach is then simpler: I just keep holding him until he is ready.

Animal research shows how the brain supports parental care, and how it can be rebuilt for it. One key region is the medial preoptic area, found deep in the hypothalamus. In California mice, for example, damage to this area reduced pup licking and made it far less likely that mice would retrieve pups, in both males and females [1]. Mothers and fathers in this species share some of the neural machinery for tending to their young.

In a 2022 study of laboratory mice, Kengo Inada and colleagues [2] found stronger connections from the lateral hypothalamus onto oxytocin-producing neurons in fathers than in sexually inexperienced males. Activating that brain pathway in inexperienced males reduced their aggression toward pups, and activating the oxytocin neurons themselves promoted caregiving. This is a far more specific view of adaptation than a brain scan can offer. Alas, it does not show how my own connections have changed. It does, however, show that fatherhood can reorganize the circuitry involved in a male’s response to offspring [2].

Human imaging points us in the same direction. Daneshnia and colleagues [3] followed 25 fathers through their infants’ first six months and observed changes in brain structure, namely reductions in gray-matter volume, most evident in the first six to nine weeks, with localized increases later. The affected regions included areas involved in understanding others and regulating behavior, and the researchers suggested that reorganization might contribute to adaptation [3]. Brain volume alone cannot tell us how well a father cares for his child, and a decrease does not by itself mean diminished ability [4].

Imaging studies of fathers are still few and recent, which says something about the need for greater understanding of fathers’ biology.

What I can say from my own experience is that I did not arrive with a story for every time he becomes upset. I learned what works for him, and that learning has to continue as his needs and interests develop.

In almost every story I tell him, someone helps the little boy, be it the animals, mama, dada, grandma, or abuela. He is never left to manage alone.

Making room

I would be giving an incomplete account if I made all of this sound effortless. There is still the sleep deprivation. Becoming a better storyteller has done nothing to eliminate the need for sleep, and the joy of being a father does not make every demand easier. We are equal partners in raising him, and his mother is his rock star. I see how much motherhood asks of her, and I am deeply grateful for the love and care she gives him. So yes, loving him deeply and finding parenthood difficult can coexist. I can yearn for time with him and still wish I had slept more.

Adaptation also involves deciding where our time and energy go. Caring for a child means making room for another person’s needs in the organization of daily life, including all the care that is needed whether or not a particular moment feels rewarding. For me, that means baths, changing him in the morning and again before bed, and putting him to bed at night, alongside the walks and the many, many books.

Testosterone research offers insight into how biology may take part in that shift. Lee Gettler and colleagues [5] followed men in the Philippines for four and a half years. Men with higher testosterone at the outset of the study were more likely to become partnered fathers. Those who did become partnered fathers then experienced larger decreases in testosterone than men who remained single nonfathers.

The authors interpret this pattern in terms of the balance between mating and parenting; time and energy spent finding mates can compete with raising offspring, and declining testosterone may help support a shift toward parental care. Among fathers, those reporting at least three hours of daily childcare also had lower testosterone than fathers reporting no involvement in care [5]. This raises the possibility that caring for a child contributes to hormonal changes and, in turn, the possibility that hormones influence caregiving itself.

For me, the shift in priorities is easy to recognize. His comfort has become something I take pleasure in providing, and making room for that care is part of how I want to spend my time.

Once upon a time

Unfortunately, the research does not yet tell us what these changes mean for how much or how well a father cares. What it does suggest is that a father’s biology is not fixed; it shifts with the experience of caring and, perhaps, in turn, helps support that caring.

This brief dive into the biology of fatherhood has made me more attentive to these small encounters. In them, my son is learning what he can expect from me, and I am learning how to be there for him. Lately, as the stories wind down, he sometimes says, “I’m good now.” There is real joy in being one of the two people he comes to for comfort.

If someone asked what we did tonight, I could say, “I told my son a story,” but that hardly captures it.

He asks for a story. I pick him up, settle him on my lap, and begin: “Once upon a time, there was a smart, kind, happy little boy…”

item.title: Keeping Your Cool: When Endless Summer Becomes a Stress Test
item.description:
Stress

Keeping Your Cool: When Endless Summer Becomes a Stress Test

Why managing heat stress is important for mental health.

Posted October 29, 2026

Key points
  • A 2025 study observed stress responses even at moderate temperatures (82.4°F).
  • Excessive heat is associated with increased risk of stroke morbidity (10%) and stroke mortality (9%).
  • Excessive heat is associated with inflammation, neuroinflammation, and sleep problems.

Though the summer has ended, the threat of excessive heat will return, and studies indicate it will get worse. Heat is certainly uncomfortable, and it can make you feel exhausted and irritable, especially when it fails to relent at night.

More than just a subjective feeling, heat stress can have a serious impact on one’s health. Excessive heat can increase the risk of major cardiovascular events like stroke and heart attack. It can also contribute to inflammation, neuroinflammation, and sleep problems. Taken together, these factors can compromise individuals’ physical as well as mental health, especially for those with an underlying condition.

This post explores the effects that heat can have on one’s wellness and is meant to serve as a reminder that your physical health and your mental health are deeply intertwined. It all begins with something that everyone has experienced: stress.

Heat as a Form of Stress

Stress is not just a subjective feeling of irritation or a sense of being overwhelmed; it has a measurable impact on blood pressure, heart rate, respiration, and other functions managed by the autonomic nervous system (ANS). The ANS is divided into two branches, the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS). The SNS is activated by stress or perceived dangers (resulting in fight-or-flight responses), while the PNS is activated when the stressor or perceived danger has passed (resulting in rest-and-digest responses). As a simple analogy, the SNS is like the gas pedal in a car, whereas the PNS is like the brake.

Activation of the SNS begins in a specific part of the brain known as the amygdala, which triggers a cascade of reactions via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the release of epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine, and cortisol. These hormones circulate throughout the body and give us the extra boost in performance we need to fight off a predator or flee to safety.

Unfortunately, stressors like heat can also activate the SNS and keep it engaged over long periods of time. A study published in 2025 by Fricke and colleagues found that even relatively mild heat exposure can lead to increased activity in the HPA axis and SNS. Specifically, they measured mean arterial pressure and heart rate, as well as concentrations of salivary cortisol and α-amylase to measure SNS arousal. They observed a stress response even at 28°C (82.4°F).

As temperature and humidity increase, it only puts more stress on the body, particularly among vulnerable populations. For context, the limit of human survivability is believed to be six hours of exposure to wet-bulb temperatures of 95°F (i.e., 100 percent humidity with an air temperature of 95°F).

The Effects of Heat Stress

Heat stress can be either acute or chronic. Acute cases of extreme heat exposure can lead to heat stroke, which is when a person’s core body temperature rises to 104°F or higher, and can result in organ failure. Common symptoms include flushing, extreme sweating, nausea, confusion, headache, agitation, rapid breathing, elevated heart rate, seizure, and coma.

As explored below, chronic heat stress can also be detrimental to health.

Cardiovascular Stress

Nonemergency heat stress can be taxing on the cardiovascular system, as the Fricke study found. That stress becomes dangerous when compounded by underlying cardiovascular conditions, but even individuals in relatively good health can be at risk of ischemic stroke and heart attack because the heat also changes blood composition, making it more predisposed to clotting—as Keatinge and colleagues astutely observed approximately 40 years ago. More recent research has corroborated the general findings of Keatinge. For example, a 2023 meta-analysis found that excessive heat is associated with a 10-percent increase in risk of stroke morbidity and a 9 percent increase in risk for stroke mortality.

Inflammation

When the SNS remains on alert for prolonged periods of time, it can activate immune pathways, leading to the release of pro-inflammatory molecules. These molecules are designed to protect against nonspecific threats to the body. When these molecules remain in circulation over prolonged periods of time, they can damage healthy tissue and increase the likelihood of inflammation and neuroinflammation. As I’ve discussed in previous posts (see here and here), the clinical correlate of neuroinflammation may be psychiatric symptoms like anxiety or depression, or cognitive symptoms like brain fog.

Sleep

Excessive heat makes it difficult to fall asleep and stay asleep because sleep requires a drop in core body temperature. When it’s too hot, people tend to move around more throughout the night, their heart rate remains elevated, they may wake up repeatedly, and they may feel as though their sleep quality is poor. This is not just a subjective feeling. REM and deep sleep stages both suffer during the heat. The body will cut short both stages of sleep if it is too hot, which can contribute to grogginess while also compromising memory consolidation, emotional health, and brain health, as the brain’s cleaning crew works most vigorously during deep sleep.

For patients with underlying psychiatric disorders, including posttraumatic stress disorder, mood disorders, or anxiety disorders, disruptions in their normal sleep schedule can exacerbate symptoms.

How to Keep Your Cool

Beyond using air conditioning, shade, or fans to cool down, it’s important to stay hydrated and to focus on sleep health when temperatures climb. Sleeping in a cool room with breathable bedding can help you get to sleep and stay asleep. Meanwhile, a warm bath or shower well before bedtime can also help the body shed heat and prime the body for sleep. Keeping your cool can also mean finding ways to de-stress through exercise, yoga, or meditation. Meanwhile, eating a diet that limits processed foods and is predominantly plant-based but contains some lean proteins like seafood, eggs, and poultry can help reduce inflammation and cardiovascular stress.

It’s important to remember that the effects of stress on the body are cumulative. Regardless of the source—whether it’s poor sleep, excessive heat, or a bad diet—stressors can negatively impact physical health and mental health. Keeping cool during the summer is not just a matter of comfort; it’s a matter of health.
